Prologue

The record, and the thing wrong with it

Two weeks ago we took the world record on Erdős minimum-overlap with a shared-tree league: two models, one PUCT search tree, each expanding the states the other found. Two arms, differing only in whether the models also teach each other directly.

armwhat it is
QG-Shared-GRPOQwen + Gemma on a shared PUCT tree — the record
QG-Shared-GRPO+CEsame, plus a cross-entropy term for sharing between the models

In code, the same thing — the shared part compressed, the difference in full:

# ---- one training step, both arms ---------------------------------
parents = tree.puct_select(k=16)

for x in parents:
    rollout["qwen"]  = qwen.sample(x, n=32)
    rollout["gemma"] = gemma.sample(x, n=32)
    tree.commit_best_child_of_each(x, rollout)

for me in ["qwen", "gemma"]:
    r = reward[me]                     # 32 rewards, my own rollouts on x
    A = r - mean(r)                    # GRPO advantage

    # ratio[i] = P_now(rollout[i]) / P_when_sampled(rollout[i])
    # corrects for the policy having moved since these were sampled;
    # exactly 1.0 on the first pass over a batch.
    loss = -sum(A[i] * ratio[i] for i in range(32))

    # ---- +CE arm only ---------------------------------------------
    you    = "gemma" if me == "qwen" else "qwen"
    better = [i for i in range(32) if reward[you][i] > max(r)]   # beats my best
    w      = normalize([reward[you][i] - max(r) for i in better])  # by how much
    loss  -= 0.1 * sum(w[i] * logprob(me, rollout[you][i]) for i in better)
    # ---------------------------------------------------------------

    adam_step(loss)

Then we found the problem. Spot preemption was silently resetting policy and optimizer weights without restoring them — the tree survived, the model did not. The record run had been restarting its policy from base at random intervals throughout training, and nobody chose that.

Consequence

The record stood, but no comparison in it was interpretable. Every arm had been taking an uncontrolled treatment.

Question one

Is restart a feature or a bug?

If accidental restarts preceded our best results, maybe dropping the policy while keeping the tree is a real mechanism. Three arms, restart as the only variable.

The convergence criterion

Derived from the four historical accidental restarts, not guessed. Let g[t] be the improvement in best-so-far attributable to step t of the current life:

restart when the newest 3 consecutive steps all satisfy   g[t] < peak / 100
where peak = the second-largest prior gain of this life (once ≥3 observations)

Two deliberate details. The peak is the second-largest, because a fresh run's first family-discovery jump is ~10³× any steady step and would make every healthy step afterwards read as 100×-decayed — firing the trigger one step after the run's biggest success. The 3-consecutive guard exists because the single-step version fired too eagerly: an earlier arm burned three restarts and finished last. Restart itself means drop LoRA weights and optimizer state, keep the tree.

Verdict

Bug, not feature. The no-restart control won outright, and the historical 50–90× recovery did not replicate. The sharpest form: the trigger correctly identified a stalled run, fired, and the restart still bought nothing — so the failure isn't trigger timing, it's that the intervention does not work under clean conditions.

Why the original observation was wrong: best-so-far is a running extremum over an append-only archive, so improvement follows every restart by construction. Measured that way the claim was unfalsifiable.

Question two

With the bug fixed, does the league still earn its cost?

Rerun the base models alone, cleanly, and see what the second model actually contributed.

Verdict

One model was enough. Q-GRPO matches the shared-tree record. The record construction genuinely contains generations from both models — but only Qwen was necessary. And the CE sharing term actively costs 3.5×10⁻⁵.

Question three

Why does the objective matter so much more for Gemma?

Reward variance is what drives the gradient, and two things set it: the model's inherent variance and the objective function.

Model inherent variance

Gemma keeps a low reward spread throughout training and almost never breaks format. Qwen has more of both.

So for Gemma, low spread means the gradient is starved — and that is exactly the regime where TTT-Discover's objective has a huge benefit.

An alternative fix that needs no new objective: raise Gemma's sampling temperature to manufacture the spread it doesn't produce naturally.

Objective function

GRPO — no std normalization A[i] = r[i] − mean(r)
TTT-Discover A[i] = max( softmax(β·r)[i] − 1, −1 )   where β solves  KL( softmax(β·r) ‖ uniform ) = ln 2
  • β ensures there is enough gradient signal even when the reward distribution is close to uniform — it is solved per group so the signal is always full-size, whatever the spread.
  • The softmax weights maximum behaviours exponentially more than those near the average.
  • The −1 floor exists because a few format failures make the variance artificially large, which would otherwise produce an extreme negative gradient that outweighs the successes.
Side effect

That floor has a consequence for Qwen. Under GRPO a format failure's advantage is proportional to how bad it is (≈ −2.3); under TTT-Discover it is clamped at −1 no matter what. The negative feedback for failing format becomes weaker and saturated — and Qwen's format failures climb over training as a result, from 10% to 30%. Gemma shows nothing of the kind under either objective, because its good formatting is inherent rather than gradient-maintained.

Two ways out

Take bigger steps

If the gradient magnitude decreases monotonically over training, raise the learning rate rather than reshaping the objective.

GRPO with β-scaling and clamping

A[i] = clamp( β·(r[i] − mean(r)), −1 )

Scales the gradient properly when rewards cluster near the average, and keeps early format failures from producing an extreme negative gradient.

Meta-discussion

TTT-Discover's main claim is that reinforcing the tail of the reward distribution is the best strategy. Combined with the PUCT tree, that may be unnecessary. Our state-tree update commits the top states per group, and in the PUCT score function those are leaves that — if the policy improved the solution — get chosen again next round. The actions we would be memorising are simply in context on the next step. Why memorise that? This points to the strength of GRPO, which reinforces general improvement rather than the maximum.

Question four

If the gradient shrinks, take bigger steps

The cheapest fix. Same objective, same batch, same budget, same tree — move only the LoRA learning rate off the inherited 4e-5 default.

Result

Q-GRPO-1.5e-4 = 0.380859354888, improving on 14 of 14 banked steps without once plateauing. The mechanism is measurable: correctness rose from 0.565 to 0.780 on average and 0.756 → 0.947 by the end — roughly 307 → 460 usable rollouts per step. More valid children mean better parents, which compounds.

A wrinkle that points at what comes next: by its final third this arm was running with advantage max 0.448, below even Gemma-GRPO's, grinding out its last improvements on a nearly flat gradient — exactly the regime where β-scaling should help most. The two fixes ought to compose.

The next hypothesis

The best model is not static

These arms define the right objective and learning rate for single-agent training. But the multi-agent hypothesis survives all of it, for a reason visible in the data: for any given problem, the best model isn't fixed.

So the question is: when models converge, does restarting with a different model help? The simple test — take the old world-record Qwen solution and train a fresh Gemma on top of it.

Meta-optimization over models

So after refining one model's best set of solutions, continue with a different model — a greedy tree search over models, where each node is a full single-agent training run.

State reuse

A. Top-K of the winning model seeds the next round.
B. Top-K across all models from the previous round seeds the next.

Policy reuse

1. Fresh model weights.
2. Continue model weights from the previous round.

Queued at depth 5 over Muse-Glimmer, Gemma and Qwen at 1.5e-4 with GRPO (no β).

Caveat

The tree-swap result above is uncontrolled — its matching Qwen-on-Qwen control was killed for grading contamination, so we cannot yet separate "the tree carried the discovery" from "Gemma is simply different."

Where this goes

Experimental plan

  • Continue to refine an optimal single-agent recipe.
  • Apply it to meta-optimization over models.
  • Apply it to multiple problems.
  • Apply it to agents.

Standing caveats

  • Single seed per arm. Contrasts inside roughly 2× are screening results. The LR win is large and mechanistically explained, but it is one run.
  • How the best-so-far curves are built. The logged pool metric is the best in the sampler's current pool, not a running extremum, so it can rise when the pool drops a state. The curves plot a true running minimum and ignore any per-step reading better than the run's own verified final tree value.
  • Variance is measured at batch granularity. Advantages are computed per 32-sample group, but the logged spread is over the whole batch. The advantage-max panel is at the right granularity; the spread panels are proxies.

Every C₅ here was recomputed from its stored construction — verifying sum(h) = n/2 exactly and matching the recomputed score to float round-trip — after we found the grader had been returning the score a program claimed rather than the one it achieved. That bug did not just corrupt numbers; in one arm it froze the search for seven steps by planting an unreachable best.
